# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization reduces rendering load by reconstructing voxel cubes from triangles and removing sides adjacent to solid neighbors, thereby avoiding the rendering of hidden geometry [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from [Isosurface extraction](30-isosurface-extraction.md) by operating on discrete block boundaries without interpolation, and from [Greedy Meshing](1776-greedy-meshing.md) by focusing on per-face visibility toggles rather than maximal quad merging. It builds on [Blocky meshing](31-blocky-meshing.md).

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate on a discrete grid $V$ where each cell $(x,y,z)$ has an occupancy state (e.g., solid/empty) or a material ID. The core geometric primitive is the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the voxel.

1.  **Discrete Representation**: The volume is represented as a 3D array. Unlike [Isosurface extraction](30-isosurface-extraction.md), no interpolation of scalar fields is performed to determine surface position; the surface lies exactly on the voxel boundaries.
2.  **Face-Based Extraction**: The primary geometric output is the set of exposed faces of the voxels. A face is exposed if the adjacent voxel in the normal direction is empty (or has a different material ID, depending on the method).
3.  **Axis-Aligned Normals**: All generated faces have normals aligned with the principal axes: $\pm \hat{x}, \pm \hat{y}, \pm \hat{z}$. This simplifies shading and culling logic compared to arbitrary normals in smooth meshing.
4.  **Culling**: A fundamental optimization is the removal of internal faces. If two adjacent voxels are both solid (and treated as the same material), the shared face is not rendered. This reduces the primitive count from $6N$ (for $N$ voxels) to approximately $2N$ for dense volumes.

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)
Dynamically updates a voxel chunk's internal state and face visibility when blocks are placed or removed, using neighbor checks to toggle shared faces without regenerating the entire mesh. It differs from [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by operating on discrete block indices and explicit face toggles rather than coverage masks [G], and from [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md) by focusing on the logical state management of block existence and face visibility rather than vertex buffer layout optimization [G].

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
Removes hidden faces of partial voxel shapes (such as stairs, slabs, or custom geometries) by representing face coverage as a bit mask. It solves the problem where a boolean "solid/empty" flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. Unlike sibling methods that rely on coarse block visibility or vertex packing, this method operates at the sub-face granularity, allowing precise culling of geometry that is occluded by neighbors while preserving exposed portions of the same face.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
Generates and maintains dynamic, face-based meshes for voxel chunks by packing vertex attributes into compact 32-bit integers and managing buffer updates via a reusable vertex slot system. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and frequent GPU buffer uploads in dynamic voxel worlds by minimizing vertex data size and enabling efficient incremental updates when blocks are added or removed. Unlike [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md), which focuses on static placement, this method provides the underlying data structure and update logic for dynamic meshing, and unlike [Mesh Reindexing and Vertex Compaction](4160-mesh-reindexing-and-vertex-compaction.md), it uses a sparse array with a free-list for vertex reuse rather than full compaction.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
Determines which discrete voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering by comparing the camera's current position and orientation against the previous frame's state, thereby avoiding unnecessary computation when the view has not changed significantly. It operates by calculating screen-space projections relative to the player's position and culling invisible faces based on surface orientation and visibility flags. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on camera-relative coordinate transformation and explicit orientation flags rather than purely geometric occlusion or coverage masks.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
A fast display method for direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a 2D boundary tracing algorithm on axis-aligned slices to determine visibility from a fixed set of viewing directions, rather than block-based culling or mask projections. It builds on [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md).

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
Filters mesh vertices and faces by projecting them into multiple camera views and checking if they fall within dilated binary masks, removing geometry not visible in any view. It differs from sibling methods like [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by operating on explicit mesh geometry (vertices/faces) rather than voxel occupancy or block placement, and from [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) by using per-pixel mask sampling instead of frustum or bounding-box tests. It is chosen when a set of reference images with associated segmentation or depth masks is available to define the visible region of interest.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
Culls mesh geometry by comparing projected vertex depths against reference depth maps rendered from multiple camera poses, classifying faces as seen, unseen, or forecast to remove artifacts from unbounded reconstructions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by using explicit multi-view depth consistency checks rather than static coverage masks, and from [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) by operating on the full mesh topology rather than spatial blocks.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The process resets the buried bitmask for the chunk, creates `MappedAdjacentChunks` for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks, and iterates through all blocks in the chunk (0 to `CHUNK_SIZE`). For each block, it determines if it is buried by calling `block->isBuried(...)` and sets the corresponding flag in the bitmask [S2, unofficial]. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via `buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()`), the mesh is marked as empty and mesh generation is skipped [S2, unofficial]. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. First, the system checks if the chunk contains any transparent blocks; if not, the second pass is skipped [S3, unofficial]. In the first (opaque) pass, if the chunk contains transparent blocks, it tests for opaque blocks (ignoring transparent and air) to generate opaque faces between air and transparent blocks; otherwise, it tests for non-air blocks [S3, unofficial]. In the second (transparent) pass, it tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks, generating faces for all transparent blocks touching air but not adding faces between transparent and solid blocks (since solid blocks already have those faces) [S3, unofficial]. To filter out solid block types during the transparent pass, before constructing the AO value and adding the block type to the hashmap, the system checks if it is in the transparent pass and ignores any block types that are not transparent [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The technique originated as a method to replace brute-force model instantiation with reconstructed cubes from triangles, improving performance by reducing the number of triangles rendered [S1, unofficial]. The initial implementation involved a class that created cubes from triangles, allowing each cube to check for solid neighbors and determine which sides to render [S1, unofficial]. To further optimize, meshes of all cubes were combined into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' [S1, unofficial]. This approach introduced constraints related to vertex limits (e.g., Unity's ~65,000 vertex limit per mesh), requiring chunks to be stacked or split [S1, unofficial]. The method is widely used in voxel-based games like Minecraft to handle tens or hundreds of chunks simultaneously, where neighboring chunks must coordinate face visibility to avoid gaps or double-rendering [S1, unofficial].
